    Neural networks in one page

    After this lesson you can explain what a neuron and a layer are, why the nonlinear activation is the whole point, and what "backpropagation" buys you — without any calculus.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~13 min Prerequisites: How models learn Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    The house-price model was a straight line: w × size + b. Straight lines are limited — most real relationships bend. A neural network is how we build models that can bend arbitrarily, while still being trainable by the exact gradient-descent loop from the last lesson. The trick is to stack many simple pieces.

    The piece: a neuron

    A single neuron does two things. First it takes a weighted sum of its inputs and adds a bias — that's just the linear model again: z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b. Then it passes that sum through a nonlinear activation function. The classic one, and the one we'll use for teaching, is ReLU ("rectified linear unit"), which is almost insultingly simple: if the number is negative, output 0; otherwise output the number unchanged. Transformers today mostly use smooth variants of the same idea (GELU, or SiLU inside a gated SwiGLU block; SmolLM2 uses SiLU), but the role is identical.

    The weights and bias are parameters — the knobs gradient descent will tune. A neuron, then, is a tiny learnable function with a kink in it.

    With real numbers: inputs 2 and −1, weights 0.5 and 1, bias 0.1. The sum is z = 0.5 × 2 + 1 × (−1) + 0.1 = 0.1, and ReLU passes it through unchanged: the output is 0.1. Had the bias been −0.1, z would be negative and the output would be 0.

    Why the nonlinearity is the entire point

    Here is the fact that makes neural networks work: if you stack linear layers with no activation between them, the whole stack collapses back into a single linear function. A line of lines is still a line. You gain nothing from depth.

    The activation breaks that. Insert a nonlinearity between layers and stacking them lets the network compose bends into bends. With enough neurons, even one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a bounded range of inputs as closely as you like (the universal approximation theorem: Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991). The theorem says nothing about how many neurons that takes or how to find the weights; gradient descent has to do that part. So the activation isn't a detail; it is the reason a "deep" network can model things a line never could.

    Key idea

    Linear layers provide capacity; the nonlinear activation provides expressiveness. Remove the activations and a 50-layer network is mathematically identical to a single linear layer.

    From neuron to layer to network

    Put many neurons side by side, all reading the same inputs, and you have a layer. Feed one layer's outputs into the next and you have a stack of layers. The layers between input and output are hidden layers — "hidden" only because you don't directly observe their values. "Deep learning" is just neural networks with several hidden layers.

    Running data left to right — input, through each layer, to the output — is the forward pass. It's the same "model(inputs)" step from the training loop, now unpacked into layer-by-layer arithmetic.

    In code, a whole layer is one matrix multiply: a grid of weights times a list of inputs gives every neuron's weighted sum at once. One of SmolLM2-135M's feed-forward layers turns 576 numbers into 1,536 that way, using a 576 × 1,536 grid of about 885,000 weights. Graphics cards are built to do huge matrix multiplies in parallel, which is why training happens on GPUs, and why parameter counts translate so directly into memory and time.

    How does it learn? Backpropagation

    Training still needs the gradient: for every one of those millions of weights, which way should it move to reduce the loss? Backpropagation is the efficient algorithm that computes all of them in a single backward sweep. Intuitively, it runs the network in reverse, distributing "blame" for the final error back through the layers — each weight learns how much it contributed to the mistake. Under the hood it is the chain rule from calculus: if the loss depends on a layer's output and that output depends on a weight, the weight's gradient is the product of the two slopes, multiplied back layer by layer (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986, Nature).

    You will essentially never implement backpropagation by hand. Frameworks like PyTorch record the operations of the forward pass and differentiate them automatically ("autograd"). What matters for you: backprop produces the gradient, and gradient descent uses it. Same loop as before — now over a network instead of a line.

    Heads up

    People say a network has "billions of parameters." Those parameters are the learned weights, counted across every layer: weight matrices like these, plus (in a language model) embedding tables and normalisation scales, and biases where the architecture has them. Many modern language models, SmolLM2 included, have no biases in their linear layers at all. Training sets all of the parameters; inference reads all of them. The saved model adds only its configuration and a few fixed, non-learned values.

    Why this matters for language

    A language model is a particular, large neural network whose inputs and outputs are about text. It has special structure — the Transformer — that we'll meet in two lessons. But it is trained by backprop + gradient descent on a loss, exactly like the toy network above. Before we get to the Transformer, we have to solve one problem: a network does arithmetic on numbers, and text is not numbers. That's the next lesson.

    Recap

    • A neuron computes a weighted sum plus a bias, then bends it with a nonlinear activation.
    • Without the activations, any stack of layers collapses into one linear function; with them, depth buys expressiveness.
    • Backpropagation (the chain rule) gives every weight its gradient, and gradient descent uses it, exactly as in the last lesson.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    (1) A neuron has inputs 1 and 3, weights 2 and −1, and bias 0.5. What does it output with ReLU? (2) Two layers with no activation: the first computes y = 2x + 1, the second z = 3y − 4. Write z in terms of x. What does that show?

    Show answer

    (1) z = 2 × 1 + (−1) × 3 + 0.5 = −0.5. ReLU turns a negative into 0, so the neuron outputs 0: it is "off" for this input. (2) z = 3(2x + 1) − 4 = 6x − 1. Two linear layers made one straight line, so the second layer added no expressiveness. Put a ReLU between them and the result can bend, which is the whole point of the activation.

    Key terms

    Neuron
    A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through a nonlinear activation.
    Weight / bias
    The learnable parameters of a neuron (many large models drop the bias).
    Activation function (ReLU)
    The nonlinearity that lets stacked layers model non-linear patterns; ReLU outputs 0 for negatives, the input otherwise.
    Layer / hidden layer
    Many neurons in parallel; hidden layers sit between input and output.
    Forward pass
    Computing outputs from inputs, layer by layer.
    Backpropagation
    The algorithm that computes the gradient for every parameter in one backward sweep, using the chain rule.
    Matrix multiply
    How a whole layer is computed at once: a grid of weights times the inputs. GPUs are built for it.
